speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Health)
text: With Singapore having one of the world's fastest ageing populations, one of its challenges is ensuring that the needs of a growing ageing population, including dental care needs, are well provided for.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Health)
text: The Singapore Dental Council (SDC) ensures that there is a steady supply of dentists each year to meet the expected demand for dental services.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Health)
text: In addition to local graduates from the Faculty of Dentistry of the National University of Singapore, the SDC also registers dental graduates from foreign universities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Against this backdrop, SDC undertook a review of the process for foreign-trained dental graduates to practise in Singapore, to ensure that they meet the same high competency standards as locally trained dental graduates.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Health)
text: SDC assessed that two measures are needed to achieve this objective.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Health)
text: This Bill gives effect to the first measure, relating to the qualifying examination, which I will explain in more detail now.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Health)
text: The second measure, which I will touch on briefly later, will be affected by way of subsidiary legislation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Under the current DRA, dental graduates from foreign universities looking to practise in Singapore will, typically, have to apply for conditional registration first.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Health)
text: This means that they have to complete a period of supervised work, usually around two years, and be assessed to be competent, before they can apply to be fully registered dentists.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Health)
text: For the purposes of an application for conditional registration, the SDC recognises dental degrees from universities in Australia, Canada, the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region, New Zealand, the Republic of Ireland, the United Kingdom and the United States of America, which are listed in the Schedule of the DRA.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Health)
text: If an applicant has a degree in dentistry from a foreign university listed in the Schedule and also meets the other prevailing criteria for conditional registration, the SDC may grant the applicant conditional registration.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Health)
text: These criteria do not currently include a requirement to pass a qualifying examination.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Health)
text: The SDC may also grant conditional registration to applicants who have degrees in dentistry from other foreign universities that are not listed in the Schedule.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Health)
text: The SDC evaluates such applications on a case-by-case basis and may require that such applicants pass an examination, to ascertain that they have the minimum skills and knowledge to practise and treat patients safely and competently in our local context.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Health)
text: This qualifying examination, which is currently already taken by foreign-trained dental graduates who do not have dentistry degrees in the Schedule, is administered by the National University of Singapore (NUS) Faculty of Dentistry and overseen by SDC.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Health)
text: It assesses a dental graduate’s clinical knowledge and procedural skills which are fundamental to the practice of dentistry.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Health)
text: This is similar in scope and benchmarked to the standards of the final-year examination of the NUS Faculty of Dentistry.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Foreign graduates who have a degree in dentistry listed in the DRA Schedule will automatically be eligible to take the qualifying examination.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Those not listed in the DRA Schedule are not automatically eligible to take the qualifying examination, but the SDC may permit them to do so on a case-by-case basis if the circumstances set out in section 14A(2) apply.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Health)
text: The treatment of foreign graduates with degrees in dentistry not listed in the DRA Schedule will not be so different from that under the current DRA in that they already have to pass an examination to be eligible for conditional registration.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Health)
text: This amendment will ensure that the competency standards of foreign dental graduates who are granted conditional registration in Singapore, whether or not their degrees are listed in the DRA Schedule, are aligned with those of dental graduates who have a Singapore degree, which means someone who has obtained a degree in dentistry from NUS.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Health)
text: This new requirement of a qualifying examination will also ensure that foreign dental graduates are familiar with the requirements for clinical practice here in Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Health)
text: For example, the local dental curriculum has, in recent times, sharpened its focus on core clinical general dentistry skills and more emphasis has been placed on geriatric dentistry, considering the trends in Singapore’s demographics.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Under the current DRA, any foreign dental graduate with a degree listed in the Schedule is entitled to be registered as a dentist with conditional registration, if he has secured employment with a local dental practice.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Health)
text: With the proposed amendment, the qualifying examination will be applicable to graduates with degrees listed in the Schedule as well.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Health)
text: To be clear, there is no change to the regime for dental graduates with a Singapore degree.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Health)
text: They continue to be eligible to apply for full registration directly.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Health)
text: There is no requirement of a qualifying examination for locally trained dental graduates.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Health)
text: This list is curated based on a review of dentistry degrees from foreign universities which the SDC deems prima facie to meet the standards for practice in Singapore, subject to the individual dental graduate’s proof of his skills, knowledge and competencies through the qualifying examination.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Health)
text: As mentioned earlier, foreign dental graduates who have a degree listed in the DRA Schedule will automatically be eligible to take the qualifying examination, unlike the foreign graduates with degrees not listed in the Schedule.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Alongside these amendments introduced by the Bill, we will be revising the Schedule to ensure that the list continues to reflect degrees in dentistry from foreign universities that give their holders this automatic eligibility to take the qualifying examination.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Health)
text: This revision will be done by way of subsidiary legislation and is actually not part of the Bill per se.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Health)
text: The Bill also makes a number of miscellaneous amendments, which are to provide for payment of penalties and composition sums into the Consolidated Fund, as well as for better administration of the Act.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Once passed, the Ministry of Health (MOH) and SDC will work closely with the dental community and other stakeholders to implement and operationalise these requirements.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Health)
text: In the coming months, SDC will engage dental students who will be affected by these changes, to ensure that they understand the new requirements and to address any concerns that they may have.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It has become necessary for Singapore to open its doors to graduates with foreign degrees in dentistry to supplement our locally trained dentists.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In doing so, it is also important to ensure that there is some standardisation in the dentistry care that is provided in the industry.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This Bill helps to ensure that we strike the right balance between opening our doors and ensuring consistency in the profession.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My first point is on the implementation of the qualifying examination for foreign degree holders.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Currently, SDC already administers a qualifying examination for graduates with foreign dentistry degrees from universities not specified in the Schedule to the Dentistry Act.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The feedback from the ground is that the qualifying examination is very stringent and the failure rates are fairly high.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I agree that we should set the bar high for the profession.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The fact that we have several graduates who are failing the qualifying examination is not a reason to lower the bar.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: With more time to practise and study, with more opportunities to attempt the examination, many dentistry graduates may, eventually, qualify and help alleviate the supply crunch facing the industry.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister share if the Ministry is considering increasing the number of attempts allowed at the qualifying examination?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister also share if the Ministry is considering increasing the duration of 12 months between attempts, even as a temporary measure, considering the present circumstances of the pandemic?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In addition, can the Minister share whether there are plans to provide increased support or training programmes for those who are struggling to pass this examination?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Dentistry is an extremely specialised degree and these graduates have spent many years applying themselves to it.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It would be a shame to end their aspirations after just two attempts at the qualifying examination, especially when it is always possible to improve.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My second point is on the alternative careers for Singaporean graduates with foreign dentistry degrees.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: While there is likely to always be a proportion of graduates who are not able to pass the qualifying examination, this group of graduates may, nonetheless, possess some meaningful skills from their years of higher education.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can MOH share if there are alternative pathways within the dentistry industry where we can channel this group of graduates into, so that these graduates can, nonetheless, pursue a career in this industry and help, again, to reduce our supply crunch?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My final point is on the present status of the dentistry industry.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is apparent from the 2019 Dental Association survey that we are some distance from easing the supply crunch.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: How effective has the measures adopted since 2017 been in easing the supply crunch?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Are there plans to further increase the local intake of dentistry students to meet the population’s dentistry care needs?

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Having the qualifying examinations ensures that the competencies of foreign graduates are aligned with the competencies of graduates holding a Singapore degree in dentistry.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: This protects the public by ensuring that only dentists who are adequately trained and qualified are eligible to start practising under conditional registration.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: This is already present in most other overseas jurisdictions and, with this, Singapore is actually aligning itself with the rest of the world.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: At this juncture, there are many young students who are already enrolled in overseas universities who are part of the Schedule.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Thirdly, I do have some queries regarding section 14A which states that “any person who does not hold a Singapore degree or a degree from a specified university may also sit for the qualifying exam if the degree the person holds is, in the opinion of the Council, not lower in standing than the specified degrees.” May I know if the Council will be having a set of objective criteria to determining the quality of these foreign degrees?

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: I am, however, glad that the Ministry said that it is going to review the Schedule and adding universities or deleting universities from the Schedule, because I believe it will have more clarity for the students who are involved.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: For example, in my work with youths, I have encountered families who have decided to send their children to study in non-accredited universities just to help them realise their children's dreams.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: This kind of clarity will allow such families to make more informed decisions when preparing for entrance examinations before university.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Similarly, in subsection (b), clarity will also be beneficial in how the Council determines if a person has “a standing that is not lower than that of a local practitioner”.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: This is because the assessment has to be made before they are permitted to even take the qualifying examinations, which aim to peg their skills to the skills of a local practitioner.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Fourthly, I would also like to clarify what sort of circumstances MOH is envisaging would be of public interest to allow a graduate to sit or not sit for the qualifying examination.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Lastly, on the basis of the qualifying examination, it is based on the final examinations and competencies criteria of the dental graduates in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: I think this is a fair benchmark to aim for.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: However, there will be instances in which these young Singaporean graduates with foreign degrees may fail this examination and this may be due to a variety of reasons.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: For example, as an orthodontist and dentist myself, I have learnt that certain dental principles have to be applied to the local context.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Dental graduates from foreign universities may not be so well-versed in, for example, the Singapore public health aspects, or that a Caucasian face would need a different treatment plan, as compared to the Asian face, or the fact that the range of common diseases changes from country to country, which means their experience and skills may differ accordingly.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: They are forced to look for alternative career pathways and maybe not even practise dentistry at all.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Another situation I feel we should think about is the fate of the young graduates with foreign degrees who come from families which are not so well-off.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: They are not able to work while doing the qualifying examination, which takes about a year to complete.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: If they fail, this may extend to another year, which may have a big impact on the family’s finances.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: A suggestion I have is to provide some sort of scaffolding for these young dental graduates who may need help in retuning their skills to the local context.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: This can be in the form of short optional courses they can apply for, which the Dental Council can conduct.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: These young graduates are, essentially, our next generation of dentists and we should give them the support they need so that we do not lose our talents, especially as we aim to raise the standard of dentistry in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Before I end, I would also like to wish a Happy Nurses’ Day to all the nurses who are such an integral part of the healthcare system, for their hard work, dedication, contributions and sacrifice, especially during this COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: This is to ensure that their competency and standards are aligned with those of local dental graduates.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Quality dental care is something which all Singaporeans will benefit from.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: However, I want to take a step back to question the current system of training dentists and the target dentist-to-population ratio.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: It appears to me that we are introducing these amendments because we do not have enough Singapore-trained dentists and we want to make sure that those who studied dentistry overseas are of a good standard.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Why do we not train more dentists in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Back in 2017, a Straits Times article had already pointed out that Singapore was not training enough dentists to meet the needs of a growing and ageing population.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: I also understand that many of those who have obtained their dentistry degree overseas are Singaporeans and PRs.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: This is not surprising as the Faculty of Dentistry at the National University of Singapore only has a small intake of 44 students in 2008, although it has increased to 80 this year.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Even then, many Singaporeans who have very good grades, many with perfect university admission score of 90 points, cannot get into dentistry.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: As a result, many of the rejected aspiring dentistry students have to ask their families to fork out a fortune for them to pursue a dentistry degree overseas.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Thus, I would like to ask the Senior Minister of State if MOH can consider increasing the capacity of the dentistry course at NUS.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: If NUS has no capacity, can we consider opening up another dental school in say, NTU, to meet the aspiration of Singaporeans and solve the insufficient supply of dentists in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Or is there an intention to restrict the numbers of locally-trained dentists?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: The question is: how do we derive the target of one dentist to 2,200 people?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Comparing to other countries’ dentist-to-population ratios, South Korea’s was one is to 2,000 in 2018; United States was one to 1,638 in 2020; Israel's was one is to 1,400 in 2017; Japan's was one is to 1,250 in 2014.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: So, is Singapore’s target of one is to 2,200 too conservative a figure?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Today, MOH recommends we consult a dentist twice a year.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: How many Singaporeans really consult a dentist every six months?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Many Singaporeans that I know of do not.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: The cost of scaling and checking your teeth by a dentist in an HDB estate will easily set you back by more than $100 and it is not mandatory for companies to provide dental benefits.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: If you want to save some money and consult a dentist at a polyclinic, it will cost you about $30 to $50 but you have to wait for months before you can make an appointment to see the dentist in the polyclinic.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Is it because MOH does not consider oral health as basic healthcare?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Or is it a way to suppress the need to increase the dentist-to-population ratio?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Meanwhile, we understand that blue Community Health Assist Scheme (CHAS), Merdeka and Pioneer Generation cardholders receive subsidies when they visit private dentists for routine check-ups.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: To make oral care more affordable, I would like to appeal to MOH to extend the subsidies to orange and green CHAS cardholders.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: At the same time, I would like to appeal to MOM to make it compulsory for all companies to provide workers with dental benefits in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: (In Mandarin):   MOH has advised Singaporeans to see a dentist twice a year.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: However, it is expensive to see a dentist.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: It would cost over $100 even if you have your teeth cleaned at a neighbourhood dental clinic.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: If you want to save money by going to a polyclinic, you will have to wait a few months before you can see a dentist.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Fortunately, blue CHAS cardholders, Merdeka and Pioneer Generation Singaporeans can enjoy subsidies when they go to private dental clinics.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: However, green and orange CHAS cardholders do not get subsidies.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Moreover, most employers do not give dental benefits to their employees.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: In other words, most Singaporeans only wait until they have a toothache before they see a dentist.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Hence, I suggest that MOH consider giving dental subsidies to green and orange CHAS cardholders.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: I also hope that MOM will also make it compulsory for employers to give dental benefits to their employees so that most Singaporeans can visit a dentist regularly and have affordable dental care.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: If Singaporeans can afford seeing a dentist, there would be a corresponding increase in the demand for dentists.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Are the current 2,475 dentists sufficient to meet the demand of Singaporeans?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: At the same time, we have to take into account the fact that an ageing population would have increased demand for dentists.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: If there is a shortage of dentists in the short term, we will need to recruit a large number of foreign graduates to make up for the shortage of local dentists.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: The Dental Registration (Amendment) Bill will make it compulsory for foreign graduates to pass the local dental examinations to ensure that their skills are comparable to those of local graduates.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: I, therefore, support the Dental Registration (Amendment) Bill.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: In the long run, NUS should consider increasing the number of dental students.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Otherwise, Singaporeans who opt to see a dentist at the polyclinic have to "dan gu gu" or "wait long long".

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: If you cannot wait and have to see a private dentist, then you have to pay "high high", and this is not ideal.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Although these diseases are less likely to cause death, they can pose significant morbidity.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We need more dentists to meet Singapore’s oral health needs, especially in the public sector.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Indeed, with an ageing population, the demand for dental services are not only increasing, but also changing due to more complex dental needs of elderly patients.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I see many seniors in my constituency who require dental care.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: For example, a resident, Mr Tan, told me that he had never visited a dentist in his life.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It was only after participating in Project Silver Screen and seeking dental care at a mobile dental clinic deployed at Yio Chu Kang CC that he discovered that he needed dental implants.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Indeed, the importance of dental care rises in old age.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Cultivating good oral hygiene habits reduces the chances of dental and other health issues in the future.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Among advanced economies, the top three countries with the largest ratio of dentists per 10,000 population are Sweden, Norway and Spain, based on the latest data available in 2018.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Sweden's ratio of dentists per 10,000 population stands at 17.9, Norway’s is 8.7 and Spain's is 8.1.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: So, we need to up our number of dentists in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: However, enrolment is very competitive, because the spaces in NUS are limited.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: From there, some stay in general dentistry or specialise.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: These range from orthodontics, prosthodontics, paediatric dentistry and so on.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Hence, the training of aspiring dentists is not just a four-year programme.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Many who cannot get enrolled into NUS have gone overseas to pursue their studies.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: First, Mr Deputy Speaker, we need to better align the professional qualifications for our dentists.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is important to have more competent and well-trained dentists in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: However, we should ensure that there is alignment in accrediting and consistency in our dentists’ professional skills.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This is because they may come from a variety of foreign universities.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Nevertheless, why is it that while their universities are listed in the approved Schedule, yet there is now a move requiring graduates from these universities to take a qualifying exam (QE) when there was none previously from the many years before?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Has there been a change in the quality of graduates from some of the universities?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Similarly, what is the timeline for the implementation of this QE?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Will the current students who have already been enrolled in these foreign universities be made to undergo a QE when they choose to return to Singapore to practise?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: There may be some anxieties that existing Singaporean dentistry students in overseas universities will be affected.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Second, Mr Deputy Speaker, the Government should consider opening up the intake for dentistry in Singapore without compromising the enrolment standards.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We only have one dental school in Singapore, in NUS.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: On the other hand, we have three medical schools in Singapore: the Yong Loo Lin School of Medicine, the Duke-NUS Medical School and the Lee Kong Chian School of Medicine at NTU.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Can we attract more foreign specialised universities to set up dental schools together with our universities?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Is it possible for NUS to increase its intake?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In this way, many of the students need not go overseas for their training.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This would, in a way, reduce the number of returning overseas dental graduates.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We all know dentistry is more than just extracting a tooth or doing an implant.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Dentists are essential in maintaining oral health in our population, especially for our seniors.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Moreover, good oral health can make a difference.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It allows one to eat well, speak well and age well.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Last but not least, it keeps that smile going.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: I will address the queries that they have raised in their speeches.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: In my opening speech, I outlined the need for a steady supply of dentists each year to meet the expected demand for dental services by Singaporeans.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng expressed concern that we need to increase our number of dentists in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Singapore, indeed, has a lower ratio of dental professionals per capita, as compared to the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) countries.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Hence, the DRA Schedule was revised comprehensively in 2008 to allow for the registration of a wider range of foreign dental qualifications.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The dental workforce has experienced a 3% to 5% year-on-year growth since then.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The student intake into the NUS Faculty of Dentistry has, historically, been derived based on targeted dentist-to-population ratios.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Predicting how many dentists we will need in the future is actually not a very easy task.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: There are factors to consider, including population demographics that evolves over time, the different dental awareness amongst the population and also the health-seeking behaviour of our people.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Singapore currently, has 0.84 visits to the dentist per capita per year.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: This is low, compared to the average of 1.3 in the OECD nations.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: We project an increase to one visit to the dentist per capita per year by 2030 and, with that, we will require a ratio of one dentist to 2,200 population by 2030.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: And we will, of course, continue to look at the evolving needs and to adjust the NUS Faculty intake where necessary.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: As pointed out by Mr Yip Hon Weng, it is important to have competent and well-trained dentists in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: All of us who ever see a dentist will want the dentist to be competent.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Currently, foreign-trained dentists who have graduated from the universities on the DRA Schedule can apply to register to practise in Singapore, if they fulfil the requirement to secure employment with a dental clinic or a healthcare institution, which is largely driven by market forces.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: This employment requirement will still be applicable when the new measures come into force.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Given the high degree of variability in overseas clinical practices and the dental curriculum of overseas universities, based either on the DRA Schedule or otherwise, the qualifying examination is, therefore, an important assessment to determine the clinical skills and competencies of a dentist, which are fundamental to the practice of dentistry and thus would ensure that the quality and competencies of foreign-trained dental graduates who are eligible to register and practise in Singapore remain high.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The qualifying examination, which is administered by the NUS Faculty of Dentistry, is benchmarked to the final-year professional dental examination that locally-trained dentists are required to pass before they can obtain their Bachelor of Dental Surgery degree from NUS.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: As such, the qualifying examination should be required for foreign-trained dentists applying for conditional registration, irrespective of their nationality.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: I turn now to address Dr Shahira Abdullah's and Mr Louis Ng's queries on the number of attempts allowed for the qualifying examination.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: To recap, the qualifying examination comprises three parts and the candidates will be provided with the qualifying examination syllabus and related preparatory materials.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: For foreign-trained Singapore Citizens and Permanent Residents who pursue dental qualifications found in the DRA Schedule and wish to practise in Singapore, there will be no cap on the number of attempts to pass each part of the qualifying examination.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: This has been the practice currently and there will be no change to this.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Historically, in the final Bachelor of Dental Surgery degree examination here in NUS, over 90% of local students passed on their first attempt and close to 100% passed by the second attempt.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Hence, a two-attempt cap for non-residents, which is the current practice, is a reasonable benchmark for ensuring the standards of those taking the qualifying examination is on par with our local graduates.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: For foreign-trained dentists, irrespective of nationality, who pursue dental qualifications not found in the DRA Schedule and wish to practise in Singapore, SDC will review their applications on a case-by-case basis and allow dentists of good repute who meet the requirements to take the qualifying examination to assess their competency to practise in the local context.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Dr Shahira Abdullah asked how SDC assesses the eligibility of foreign-trained dentists who do not hold a Singapore degree or a degree from a university specified in the DRA Schedule, to sit for the qualifying examination.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: As stated in the DRA, this is left to SDC's discretion.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: SDC has, generally, allowed foreign-trained dentists to take the qualifying examination so long as the university from which they attained their basic dental degree is recognised by the respective dental regulatory body of the country.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The teaching medium is in English, failing which, the dentist must take and pass an English Language proficiency test.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: And thirdly, if they meet other requirements, like having an offer of employment and whether the foreign-trained dentist has a connection to Singapore, such as being a Singaporean/Permanent Resident (PR) or married to a Singaporean/PR or children of PRs, for example, as published on SDC's website.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: This means that students who are currently enrolled in or have secured places in dentistry courses overseas and will graduate before 1 January 2029, as well as foreign-trained dental graduates who already hold basic dental qualifications from universities on the DRA Schedule will not be affected by this change and will be considered for conditional registration to practise dentistry in Singapore if they fulfil the requirements under the current DRA.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Mr Yip Hong Weng has asked for clarification on why the Ministry does not just refine the current DRA Schedule by removing universities that do not produce graduates on par with local graduates, instead of imposing this qualifying examination.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: In relation to the DRA Schedule, the SDC has reviewed local and overseas practices to assess the clinical competence and eligibility of a dentist for registration.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Jurisdictions, such as Canada, Hong Kong SAR and Thailand have adopted a national examination regime for foreign-trained dentists.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Countries, such as Norway and Germany, use a Schedule of schools with exemptions on a case-by-case basis for non-citizens.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Countries, such as Denmark, Ireland, Sweden, United Kingdom, United States of America, Australia and New Zealand have adopted a hybrid of Schedule and national examination, based on citizenship, location of dental training or licence.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: And as Dr Shahira Abdullah has pointed out, the QE is, in fact, present in many overseas jurisdictions and, with these amendments, Singapore would be in alignment with the rest of the world.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Additionally, SDC has reviewed the international rankings of the 89 universities in the DRA Schedule.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Most of the top-ranked schools in the latest international rankings, which are primarily based on academic/employer reputation and research citations, are not in the DRA Schedule.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Together with the variation in dental practices and training across overseas universities, international rankings would, therefore, be less relevant for the purpose of removing universities that may not produce foreign dental graduates on par with local graduates.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: I must clarify that, in contrast to what Mr Ang Wei Neng has said earlier, MOH actually has no guidance for a twice-a-year visit to a dentist.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: In fact, we are already moving to a risk-based approach, which is what is practised in the UK as well.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: For example, those who are deemed to have low dental risks actually may only need to see the dentist once every two years.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: So, this is more of a risk-based approach.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: And in the context of our local practice, we also have upstream basic care given to students in the schools.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: So, it is to be seen in the context of a holistic dental care ecosystem and not just at the primary care level, when the person has become an adult.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: MOH monitors and reviews primary care dental capacity provided by private CHAS dental clinics and public polyclinics, both of which provide subsidised dental services.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: There are, currently, over 800 CHAS dental clinics islandwide.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Pioneer Generation, Merdeka Generation, as well as Community Health Assist Scheme (CHAS) Blue and Orange card holders, enjoy subsidies for selected basic dental services at private CHAS dental clinics.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Singaporeans can also look forward to dental services in the upcoming polyclinics, such as Bukit Panjang and Eunos Polyclinic, which are scheduled to open this year.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Their questions and comments have provided valuable insight on the areas that we should focus on when implementing these measures.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: I should reiterate that, as I have mentioned in my speech earlier, for these proposed measures to ensure the continued quality of foreign-trained dentists seeking to practise in Singapore, we will need the support of the dental community to help implement and operationalise these amendments.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: I am confident that these amendments will go a long way to ensure the continued high quality of foreign-trained dentists to complement our dental workforce in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah
text: Moving forward, may I ask if the Ministry will consider reviewing the DRA Schedule more regularly because the last one was actually quite a while back and a lot of things have changed since then.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: But I think that the key is in the fact that dentistry is more of a practice where you actually do things with your hands, whereas the ranking of dental schools is not necessarily in conjunction with the quality of the practice of the person but more so depending on citations, research outputs, which does not necessarily translate into actual dental practice.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: So, the reputation of the school itself could well be more biased towards academia and research.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: So, that leads me to the Member's second question, which is, when will SDC be the one that takes a case-by-case approach.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: But if you are a non-Singapore/PR, you may only take it with a cap of two times within a 12-month period.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: For those that SDC needs to make a decision, those are graduates who are not within the list itself, that means, if you take a degree that is outside the Schedule list, then you will need to have SDC look upon your application on a case-by-case basis, before the person can be allowed to take the qualifying examination.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: I hope that clarifies the Member's questions.      .
